newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA sees Australia inflation under 2.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA sees Australia inflation under 2.5 pct.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said on Wednesday it expected underlying inflation to remain under 2.5 percent for the rest of 1996/97 to June 30 and that it expected a good inflation performance for 1997/98.

The RBA said the strength in the exchange rate had been a factor in the good inflation outlook, but that it remained above its average of recent months. It also said it believed the economy had the capacity to grow a little faster without putting pressure on inflation. Earlier, it cut official cash interest rates by half of a percentage point to 6.0 percent.
The RBA said however that monetary policy assumed that wages growth would remain consistent with inflation in the two to three percent range.
"Following the considerations at the Board meeting last week the Bank will operate in the money market today to reduce the cash rate from 6.5 percent to 6.0 percent," the RBA said.

"This reduction essentially reflects a further improvement in the inflationary outlook. The bank now expects underlying inflation to stay below 2.5 percent for the remainder of this financial year, and our assessment is for continued good inflation performance in 1997/98," it said.
"This improvement in the inflation outlook is influenced by the strength of the exchange rate which, despite the volatility of last week, remains above its average of recent months," the RBA said.
"There is also further evidence from surveys of reductions inflationary expectations, and the price deflators in the latest National Accounts confirm further falls in actual inflation."
It said recent figures had had little effect on its assessment of economic growth in aggregate, "although the balance is slightly altered."
The RBA said confidence that investment would be a source of strength over the next year had increased, while the outlook for consumption was a little more subdued.
"Overall, it is the bank's assessment that the economy has the capacity to grow a little faster without putting pressure on inflation," it said.
"Today's easing, together with the two earlier ones, should provide an environment for stronger employment growth, subject to appropriate wage restraint."
The bank cut official rates on July 31 and November 6 by half a percentage point on each occasion.
The RBA said monetary policy remained focussed on longer term factors like inflation.
"Here the outlook for labour costs remains crucial. At present, aggregate wage developments are consistent with inflation staying at a 2 to 3 per cent average," it said.
"Monetary policy is assuming, for the time being, that this will remain the case," the bank said.
However, if wages growth were to rise appreciably because of enterprise bargains or centralised decisions there would be a severe squeeze on business, the RBA said.
"Monetary policy would, in such circumstances, be set to preserve the favourable outlook."
